newsitem.title: GERMANY: German metal employers fail to cut sick pay costs.
newsitem.headline: German metal employers fail to cut sick pay costs.

text.p: Germany's largest metal and engineering employers on Wednesday signed wage agreements for 1997 that failed to put into effect a new law designed specifically to offer them deep cuts in sick pay costs.

The back-down follows fierce protests by hundreds of thousands of workers over the last two months and means that the reduction in labour costs that industry bosses have for years been crying out for will have to be postponed yet again.

Negotiators in the large steel-making region of North Rhine-Westphalia said on Wednesday they had reached a wage deal guaranteeing continued full sick pay for the 850,000 metal workers in the region, the largest in a sector employing a total 3.2 million workers.
North Rhine-Westphalia is home to German steel giants Thyssen AG and Krupp-Hoesch Stahl.

The accord came as employers in the southern part of the state of Baden-Wuerttemberg, home to companies such as Daimler Benz AG's car-making unit Mercedes, said they had signed a similar pact with some 300,000 workers there.

In neighbouring Bavaria, where some 650,000 workers are employed, union leaders said they were also confident of a deal maintaining sick pay costs and warned of renewed industrial action if employers did not make acceptable offers.
"The path to possible industrial action would be a fast one to go down," a Bavarian IG Metall official said.

The newly-signed packages are based on a break-through deal signed last week in the northern state of Lower Saxony guaranteeing full sick pay and a 1.5 percent rise in 1997 followed by 2.5 percent increase in 1998.

In return, employers demanded a five percentage point cut to workers' traditionally generous Christmas bonuses to 55 percent of one month's salary, making the overall labour cost increase in 1997 less than one percent.

While that is well short not only of past wage agreements in the sector but also IG Metall's original 4.5-5.0 percent wage claim for 1997, employers had been hoping that the sick pay cuts would have helped trigger much wider cuts in labour costs.

Some have gone as far as saying labour costs in the sector need to be reduced by 20 percent over the coming years if they are not to pull production out of Germany and relocate it to other, lower-cost countries.
The new package in North Rhine-Westphalia goes a small step further than the Lower Saxony deal in reducing costs by tying Christmas bonuses to the level of absenteeism in a company.
Such bonuses there could now slip to 50 percent for firms where there is a particularly high rate of absenteeism.
And in Bavaria, employers are seeking an arrangement under which they will be able to reduce working hours, and their staff wage bill accordingly, in companies facing stagnant business conditions.
But they said as talks continued on Wednesday that they are resigned to having to pay full sick payments in the coming year.
